desc:
Given a lowercase string s, count how many different strings can be produced by reordering its characters (the original order counts as one of them). Equal strings are counted once, even if they come from different orderings of identical letters.

Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

s = "aab"  ->  3   ("aab", "aba", "baa")
s = "abc"  ->  6
s = "aaaa" ->  1
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: If all letters were different, there would be n! orderings. What changes when a letter appears several times?
Swapping two equal letters does not change the string, so every distinct string is counted c! times for a letter occurring c times (for each letter independently).
The answer is n! / (ca! cb! ...). Precompute factorials modulo the prime and divide using modular inverses (Fermat: xp-2).
editorial: Count the orderings of the n positions as if every character were distinguishable: n!. A given resulting string corresponds to exactly c1! · c2! · ... of these orderings, since the occurrences of each letter can be permuted among their positions freely. So the number of different strings is the multinomial coefficient n! / ∏ ci!.

Since the modulus is prime, division is multiplication by the modular inverse, computed with pow(x, MOD - 2, MOD). Building n! takes O(n) multiplications, plus at most 26 inverses. Total O(n + 26 log MOD) time, O(1) extra space beyond the factorial loop.
